paras: The threatened lynching of Arthur Reese occurred in Moundsville, West Virginia, on the evening of June 27, 1903, when a crowd in the mayor's office cried for the lynching of Reese, a Black coal miner accused of cutting a white painter, Pat Rowan. No attempt was reported; Reese was jailed and held for the grand jury.

According to the Wheeling Sunday Register, the trouble began about five o'clock in the Arlington saloon, where someone knocked a sandwich from Reese's hand, "either purposely or accidentally," and a row followed.

Witnesses differed on whether the cutting happened inside or on the sidewalk; Reese, thrown from the bar room, landed holding an open knife, and Rowan was cut across the side and arm. Rowan's brother Jack, a barber, caught Reese down the avenue and took him to the mayor's office, where a large crowd gathered and "numerous cries of 'Lynch the nigger'" were heard. Jack Rowan then fetched a pistol to shoot Reese but was disarmed by others, and Reese was taken to jail.

At a preliminary hearing on June 29 before Squire Hammond, Reese, named as "Arthur Reeves," denied the cutting but was held in $500 for the grand jury on a charge of assault. On his attorney's advice he went to jail rather than seek bond; no report of grand jury action or a trial was found.

The Sunday Register headlined the story "CROWD CRIED 'LYNCH NIGGER'," called the cutting a "dastardly assault," and described Reese as "a dangerous colored man" without giving his side. The daily Register's June 30 follow-up recorded his denial and omitted the crowd; the Ceredo Advance's July 1 state-news column gave three sentences marking Reese "colored" and Rowan "white." Only these West Virginia white papers carried the case; no Black-press report of it was found.

The Register called the wound "not thought to be dangerous," but the Ceredo Advance said Rowan "can not survive" and that "the entire police force" was needed to prevent a lynching, where the Register said no attempt was made. Reese's assault-only charge two days later favors the local account of Rowan's condition.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Arthur Reese
bases: A large crowd in the Mayor's office cried for the lynching of a Black prisoner accused of cutting a white man, and the victim's brother fetched a pistol to shoot him; no attempt was carried out (A1, A3).

Reese was not killed: the crowd's cries and Jack Rowan's pistol came to nothing and Reese was jailed and held for the grand jury (A1, A2); the episode is a threatened lynching by a large crowd acting on a crime accusation (A1, A3).

Two different papers, the Wheeling Sunday Register and the Ceredo Advance, report the cutting and the lynching threat in differing words and detail, so the brief is not a verbatim reprint, though it may derive from Wheeling reports (A1, A3); the daily Wheeling Register confirms the arrest and hearing (A2).

accounts.label: Local report (Wheeling Sunday Register)
accounts.gist: A row began after someone knocked Reese's sandwich away; Reese, thrown from the saloon with an open knife, is said to have cut Rowan; a crowd cried for lynching but no attempt was made, and the wound was not thought dangerous.

accounts.label: Accused at hearing
accounts.gist: Reese denied cutting Rowan; Rowan and witnesses who saw a knife in his hand said otherwise.

accounts.label: State-news brief
accounts.gist: Reese stabbed Rowan in a row over a sandwich; Rowan cannot survive; the entire police force was needed to prevent a lynching.

framing.detail: The Sunday Register headlined the crowd's slur ('CROWD CRIED "LYNCH NIGGER"'), said 'Fortunately' no attempt was made, but called the cutting a 'dastardly assault', praised Jack Rowan's reputation, and called Reese 'a dangerous colored man'.
The daily Register's 'Held to Grand Jury' item reported the hearing and Reese's denial without mentioning the crowd.
The Ceredo Advance's 'State News Items' gave three sentences marking Reese 'colored' and Rowan 'white' and stressing the police effort to prevent a lynching.

versions.value: Wound 'ugly' but 'not thought to be dangerous'; Rowan able to go about a few hours later

conflicts.note: The local Register is the better evidence: two days later Reese was charged only with assault and no grave condition was mentioned (A2).

Arlington saloon on Lafayette avenue, then the Mayor's office, Moundsville
Arthur Reese (spelled 'Arthur Reeves' in the hearing report), described as 'a negro coal miner' and 'colored'
Accused of cutting Pat Rowan, a white painter, across the left side and right arm with a knife after a row over a sandwich; charged with assault
A large crowd that collected in the Mayor's office; Jack Rowan, the cut man's brother, fetched a pistol intending to shoot Reese
